holes.why: Two search sweeps on 2026-08-04 found no such product. The only garden-bed-scale seeder ($7,995, 18 sq m) is roughly two orders of magnitude off on coverage-adjusted cost, and field-scale machines ($60,000, 20-30 hectare design targets) are priced for plots 80 to 120 times larger than a quarter acre. The attack cannot be grounded; it is recorded here so the search is repeatable.

prose.text: [[passage: p1 | No commercially available autonomous seeder can plant a quarter-acre plot for less than ten times the cost of hired labor in its first season / The cheapest garden-scale autonomous seeder sells for $7,995 / That seeder's maximum footprint is 3 by 6 meters, 18 square meters / Field-scale autonomous seeders cost about $60,000 and are designed for fields of 20 to 30 hectares / Hired crop labor costs $17.15 per hour at the US median / A walk-behind push seeder plants a full 30-inch bed in one or two walking passes | ~102w]]
[[passage: p2 | A commercially available seeder exists that plants a quarter acre cheaply enough to bring the gap under tenfold | ~12w]]
[[passage: p3 | FarmBot's maker publishes an ROI analysis showing the robot pays for itself | ~17w]]
[[passage: p4 | Even by the vendor's own ROI analysis, measured against retail produce prices, FarmBot's direct-cost payback takes years, not one season | ~17w]]

Nothing you can buy today will seed a small plot for less than hired hands cost. The cheapest garden robot on the market runs $7,995 and tends a footprint of just 18 square meters. Machines built for real fields, like the $60,000 FarmDroid, are designed for farms of 20 to 30 hectares. Meanwhile a farm worker earning the median $17.15 an hour, pushing a Jang seeder, finishes a bed in two passes.

No commercially available autonomous seeder can plant a quarter-acre plot for less than ten times the cost of hired labor in its first season. The cheapest garden-scale autonomous seeder sells for $7,995. That seeder's maximum footprint is 3 by 6 meters, 18 square meters. Field-scale autonomous seeders cost about $60,000 and are designed for fields of 20 to 30 hectares. Hired crop labor costs $17.15 per hour at the US median. A walk-behind push seeder plants a full 30-inch bed in one or two walking passes.
A seeder that plants a quarter acre cheaply enough to bring the gap under tenfold does not exist.
FarmBot's maker publishes an ROI analysis showing the robot pays for itself, but against retail produce prices, not hired planting labor.
Even by the vendor's own ROI analysis, measured against retail produce prices, FarmBot's direct-cost payback takes years, not one season.
